meta.dataset: On The Door — pilot council sources registry
meta.regime_note: England & Wales: Cumulative Impact Policies/Assessments under Licensing Act 2003 (CIAs renew every 3 years, SoLPs every 5). Scotland: overprovision assessments under Licensing (Scotland) Act 2005. London boroughs: the Mayor of London's strategic licensing powers under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 CAME INTO FORCE ON 29 JUNE 2026, two months after Royal Assent. In force now: a statutory duty on every London licensing authority to consult the Mayor when determining or revising its Statement of Licensing Policy, and a Responsible Authority role for the GLA (City Hall can make representations on individual applications and appeal to the magistrates' court). Still awaited: the London-wide Strategic Licensing Policy itself and the Mayor's call-in power over strategically important decisions — both require secondary legislation the government says will be laid later in 2026. (Checked 1 Oct 2026: the GLA project page still describes the powers in the future tense and still says the call-in secondary legislation is 'expected to be laid and passed later this year'; no instrument found.)

status_key.tightening: New/expanded CIA, SCZ, or live consultation likely to restrict
status_key.stable: Policy in force, no active change
status_key.loosening: CIA/overprovision removed or presumption of refusal dropped

councils.name: Westminster City Council
councils.policy: Statement of Licensing Policy October 2026 ADOPTED by Full Council 16 Sep 2026, published 28 Sep, IN FORCE 1 OCT 2026 (verified on the council's own page). West End CIZ RETAINED but REDUCED on its western, eastern and northern edges (substantial parts of Covent Garden, Mayfair and north of Oxford Street taken out); Core Hours reworded as 'reference points rather than fixed limits'; new definition of 'Vertical Drinking' (little or no seating, customers predominantly stand) retained despite the backlash; VAWG and Martyn's Law provisions; expanded Good Operator Guidance (Sep 2026). Council commits to a 12-18 month review of the CIZ and Core Hours evidence base and an industry expert panel. The Mayor had asked for the CIZ to be dropped entirely - not followed.
cia_zones: West End CIZ (retained, reduced on W/E/N edges - in force 1 Oct 2026)
Mayfair / Victoria special zones (reported in the draft; NEEDS VERIFICATION against the adopted 121-page policy)
Edgware Road and Queensway/Bayswater CIZs (draft proposed removal; NEEDS VERIFICATION against the adopted policy)

live_consultation.subject: SoLP 2026 consultation closed 9 Aug (690 responses vs 170 in 2021); policy adopted 16 Sep, in force 1 Oct 2026

councils.notes: 1 OCT 2026 - ADOPTED, AND THE PAGE IS FINALLY UNFROZEN. Full Council adopted the Statement of Licensing Policy 2026 on 16 SEPTEMBER; published 28 Sep (council page) and IN FORCE TODAY, 1 OCTOBER 2026 - so the long-flagged 1 Oct date is now VERIFIED on the council's own page and the flag is closed. The SoLP page was updated 29 Sep: it now carries the October 2026 policy (PDF, 121pp), Good Operator Guidance Sept 2026 and the 2021 policy 'until 1 October'. Small aggregation-gap exhibit: the rewritten page refers to 'the Licensing Act 2033'. WHAT CHANGED (Poppleston Allen 17 Sep; Morning Advertiser 17 Sep; CLH 18 Sep): West End CIZ shrunk on W/E/N edges; Core Hours now 'reference points rather than fixed limits'; vertical drinking definition retained; VAWG + Martyn's Law; enforcement detail; 690 responses vs 170 in 2021 (council report attributes the rise partly to 'misunderstandings'); council calls the policy 'broadly similar' to 2021 because of the compressed statutory timetable and commits to a 12-18 month review of the CIZ and Core Hours evidence plus an industry expert panel. Committee papers published 7 Sep (MA 9 Sep, citing the Guardian): 81% of respondents disagreed with the CIZ and 84% said the policy would be bad for business. THE MAYOR: asked for the CIZ to go entirely; it stays, smaller. Khan (MA 9 Sep): 'breathtaking arrogance... They would rather see nightlife die than thrive', and backed the call-in power. Cllr Tim Barnes: called on the Mayor to reverse Met licensing team cuts, extend night buses and run a Thursday Night Tube. DIRECTION CHANGE tightening -> MIXED: this is a NEW EVENT (adoption), not a correction - smaller CIZ and benchmark-only core hours are loosening moves, while the retained vertical-drinking definition and seating/table-service steer tighten. NOT YET VERIFIED from the adopted document itself (121pp, 28MB; could not be text-extracted this run): whether Edgware Road / Queensway CIZs were removed as drafted and whether Mayfair / Victoria special zones survived. Also 9 Sep: Trisha's (New Evaristo Club, Greek St) granted 2am inside the CIZ over a Met objection; Mistress of Mayfair kept its licence on review with conditions. || 1 SEP 2026 - OUR TOP WATCH QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND WE HAD MISSED THE ANSWER. Last run we recorded as NEEDS VERIFICATION whether Westminster had consulted the Mayor and what he said, and wrote that nothing on any council page addressed it. The council pages still don't. But the Mayor had already written, and it was reported on 10 AUGUST 2026 - two weeks before our last run. We were interrogating council websites and not the trade press on that specific question. Recording the miss rather than quietly filling it in. WHAT HE ASKED FOR: Sir Sadiq Khan wrote to the Conservative-run council asking it to lift its core hours restrictions and to DROP THE CUMULATIVE IMPACT POLICY ENTIRELY - the West End CIZ, the most closely watched cumulative impact area in the country - arguing the council should set out a vision for the growth it wants rather than a list of activity it wants to limit. Evidence he deployed: London nightlife supports 600,000+ jobs and adds upwards of GBP 21bn to the UK economy annually; and Home Office figures showing only 41 licence applications were made in the West End cumulative impact area in 2023-24, of which just 16 were approved. He named MANCHESTER - no core hours policy, no cumulative impact policy - as the model, which is the contrast this dataset has drawn since launch. He accused the council of letting licensing decisions be shaped disproportionately by a small number of vocal residents and councillors. NEW DRAFT DETAIL not previously in this entry, from the same coverage: preferential treatment for operators closing by 10pm, with newly licensed pubs stopping service at 10pm and new nightclubs closing 11.30pm weekdays and midnight weekends; and separate special policy areas proposed for MAYFAIR and VICTORIA. Treated as reported, not verified against the draft. WESTMINSTER'S REPLY: deputy leader Cllr Tim Barnes said licensing is not the primary concern operators raise - central government costs, bills and staffing are - and pointed to reduced policing and gaps in late-night public transport, both within the Mayor's own remit. PAGE STILL FROZEN, FOURTH CONSECUTIVE CHECK. Fetched in full 1 Sep: last updated 29 June; opens 'Westminster City Council is consulting on proposed changes'; still states 'The consultation closes on 9 August at 5pm' in the present tense with the Commonplace documents and the survey both linked live. Twenty-three days after it closed. It also still serves the October 2021 policy as current. STILL NEEDS VERIFICATION: the 1 Oct 2026 adoption date. Trade coverage now describes the draft as being consulted on 'ahead of its planned introduction on 1 October 2026', which strengthens it, but no council page confirms it and the council's own 4 Mar 2026 release spoke of developing updated policies 'over the coming year'. Not asserted.
councils.next_review_due: 12-18 month review of CIZ + Core Hours evidence promised (to ~early 2028) · SoLP 2031

EIGHTEEN MONTHS and still no mention of the Shoreditch CIA or the Dalston Special Consideration Area anywhere in the body - what the policy covers, why the activities are licensed, how to apply, and nothing else. councils.policy: SoLP 2025-2030 adopted; cumulative impact areas (Camden Town, Seven Dials) REMOVED - committee found insufficient evidence for a CIA. Late Night Levy retained and EXTENDED to late night refreshment premises (00:00-05:00); the fee-free opt-out window CLOSED 31 AUG 2026 and non-opted premises are now liable, pro rata from licence anniversary
councils.notes: 1 OCT 2026 - THE CAMDEN REVIEW DOWNGRADED. Second run without locating the sub-committee's own decision record; per last run's rule the notice is retired from the board and carried only as 'reported, unverified'. LNR opt-out take-up still unpublished (phone/FOI). Levy page re-read 1 Oct: 'late night refreshment' still absent. SoLP page resolves (2025-2030, expires 23 Jul 2030). || 1 SEP 2026 - THE DEADLINE PASSED AND THE COUNCIL'S PAGE NEVER MENTIONED IT. The fee-free opt-out from the extended Late Night Levy closed on Sunday 31 August 2026. Late night refreshment premises that did not submit a minor variation cutting their LNR hours are now liable, charged pro rata from their licence anniversary. camden.gov.uk/late-night-levy was pulled in full again on 1 September, the day after: it STILL runs only the 2016 alcohol-only scheme - 'All licence holders operating a licence which allows for the sale of alcohol between midnight and 6am are required to pay into the levy', the three exemptions, 'No other exemptions apply', the s.55A suspension warning. The phrase 'late night refreshment' does not appear on it once. No opt-out route, no deadline, at any point in the five weeks we checked it. This is now a completed aggregation-gap case study rather than a live warning. SECOND STALE CAMDEN PAGE, NEW THIS RUN: camden.gov.uk/late-night-levy-review-consultation is still in the present tense - 'We are now holding a 6-week public consultation' - and still says 'Your views will inform recommendations to Full Council in March 2026', six months after that Full Council sat and decided. Added as a source for exactly that reason. It does carry detail available nowhere else: the review was conducted independently by SixTillSix Ltd and MAKE Associates; the levy funds 72 hours of additional high-visibility policing every week; it had not been reviewed since introduction in 2016; and the adopted package includes appointing a Late-Night Manager/Coordinator, an annual report to Licensing Committee, monthly police updates to the LNL consultative group, and retention of the 70/30 split to the Met and the council. NOT ON THE PUBLIC RECORD, NEEDS A CALL OR AN FOI: how many LNR premises actually opted out by 31 August, and whether the promised letter to licence holders went out. LICENCE REVIEW IN THE BOROUGH: The Camden (Camden Town) - sub-committee imposed conditions rather than revoking, reported 18 Aug 2026, after Met representations alleging a 'culture of non-compliance' including two unreported violent incidents in one night. Conditions reported as electronic ID scanning after 8pm, CCTV upgrade with 31-day retention, more SIA door staff including female staff at peak hours, a digital incident log, and training for senior staff and the DPS within 30 days. Primary committee record not located; carried on local press. Direction unchanged - a review outcome is not a policy move. Direction remains MIXED (CIA removal loosening, levy extension tightening), unchanged since 27 Jul 2026.

councils.notes: 1 OCT 2026 - LIVE CONSULTATION, AND WE MISSED IT FOR TWO RUNS. Bristol opened a consultation on 22 JULY 2026 on whether to RETAIN the city-centre CIA (Cabot Sector incl. Welsh Back and Stokes Croft); it CLOSES MIDNIGHT WEDNESDAY 14 OCTOBER 2026. The council's own consultation page states the existing CIA expires 7 MARCH 2027 (we had carried 'Mar 2027'). It sat on the council's 'Ask Bristol' finder throughout August while we were checking the licensing-policy page, which - re-read 1 Oct in the browser - still does not mention it. Same failure mode as the Mayor's letter: we watched the page that ought to carry it, not the page that does. Survey: smartsurvey.co.uk/s/CIA2026. Direction stays STABLE: a consultation on retaining an existing CIA is not a move to restrict; if the council proposes extension or removal that changes. Note also the old 2020 citizenspace CIA consultation still surfaces in search and reads as live - it closed 28 Oct 2020. || EL RINCÓN DECIDED 20 AUG 2026. After a four-hour hearing the licensing sub-committee unanimously took NO ACTION beyond requiring CCTV inside and outside, plus a recommended sign identifying the venue as a home fans' bar. It REFUSED the police's requested conditions — alcohol only with a main meal (which would have ended vertical drinking at the premises) and a ban on serving drinks in glasses. Cllr Richard Eddy: it had not been proven that El Rincón contributed to unrest and disorder; unfair to make the licensee wholly responsible for matchday incidents in the area; 'We were not convinced by the police's case on vertical drinking so we are not going to impose a condition that bans that. It's a wonderful business.' Review ref 26/03363/PRREV, valid 18 Jun 2026, reps closed 16 Jul, hearing held seven days outside the 20-working-day window that expired 13 Aug. LINK FIX 24 AUG 2026 (monthly run): the policy URL we carried, bristol.gov.uk/licences-permits/licensing-policy, now 301s to bristol.gov.uk/business/licences-and-permits/licensing-policy — the council has restructured its business section. Not broken, but no longer canonical; source updated to the destination. Content re-verified on the new page: 'The last full policy review took place in 2025 and the policy came into effect on 1 August 2025', Cumulative Impact Assessment linked from the same page. CIA 2024–2027 (approved 29 Feb 2024, effective 8 Mar 2024) unchanged, city centre CIA in place. Direction stays STABLE — a review outcome is not a policy move, but note the outcome cuts the same way as the national row: a licensing committee declining, on the evidence, to regulate standing. LINK CHECK 1 SEP 2026 (monthly run): source URL re-surfaced by site-restricted search and re-fetched; page resolves and content matches this entry. Held. The restructured /business/ path is holding as canonical; CIA renewal remains due by Mar 2027.

live_consultation.subject: Statutory consultation on REVOKING the Late Night Levy - closed; Full Council decision pending (reported 7 Oct), proposed end date 31 Oct 2026

councils.notes: 1 OCT 2026 - CONSULTATION CLOSED 22 SEP, DECISION PENDING. Let's Talk Newcastle now reads 'This consultation has now ended'; decision 'will be published later this year'. Full Council date of 7 Oct carried from last run's sources - not re-confirmed against a published agenda this run (NEEDS VERIFICATION). Direction stays MIXED pending the vote; revert to stable if refused. The council's own Late Night Levy page, re-read 1 Oct in the browser, STILL advertises the independent-review consultation 'by 17 July 2026' and still says nothing about the revocation proposal, the closed statutory consultation or the 31 Oct end date - eleven weeks stale. || DIRECTION CHANGE 1 SEP 2026: stable -> MIXED, and it is the first movement on the board since Birmingham on 24 August. Newcastle City Council's Licensing Committee met on 24 AUGUST 2026 - hours after our last run published - and agreed to recommend that the Late Night Levy be REVOKED, proposed end date 31 October 2026. The review report to that committee recorded 93% of respondents supporting abolition. A statutory consultation on revocation is live and CLOSES 22 SEPTEMBER 2026; Full Council decides 7 October. Levy facts from the council's own 19 Aug release: in place since 2013, managed with the Northumbria Police and Crime Commissioner; 281 premises; GBP 299 to GBP 4,400 a year; GBP 3.46m raised since 2013, of which GBP 2.26m to the PCC and GBP 968,432 to the council; funds street cleansing, CCTV, Street Marshals, Taxi Marshals, the Safe Haven van on Bigg Market and extra police patrols. Leader Cllr Colin Ferguson (new Liberal Democrat administration): 'this Cabinet does not think it is fair that Newcastle is one of just two cities outside of London that expects hospitality venues to contribute towards policing and public safety initiatives.' Replacement proposed: a new governance structure funded by the council and the NE1 Business Improvement District. WHY MIXED AND NOT LOOSENING: the five cumulative impact policy areas introduced by the 2023 SoLP review remain in force and unchanged - a tightening posture - while a live consultation proposes removing a financial burden on the late-night trade. Our own status key counts a live consultation likely to restrict as tightening, so a live consultation likely to relax is treated the same way in reverse. That is the same reasoning applied to Camden on 27 July, in the opposite direction. This is a proposal, not an adopted change: if Full Council refuses on 7 October, Newcastle reverts to stable. AGGREGATION GAP, AND A GOOD ONE: the council's own Late Night Levy page (fetched in full 1 Sep) carries none of it. It still advertises the EARLIER independent-review consultation under the heading 'Late Night Levy consultation' with 'To take part - by 17 July 2026', six weeks after that closed, and the hyperlink offered to take part points back to the same page - a self-referential loop. No mention of the 24 August decision, the 22 September statutory consultation, or the proposed 31 October end date. A Newcastle licensee wanting to comment on whether their own levy is abolished cannot get there from the council's levy page. SoLP page itself re-checked and unchanged: 'Licensing Act 2003 - Statement of Licensing Policy', SoLP 2023-2028. CROSS-REFERENCE: the council's release states Newcastle and LIVERPOOL are the only cities outside London charging a levy. Both are pilot authorities. If Newcastle revokes on 7 October, Liverpool becomes the last one standing.
